questions.question: The line graph shows the temperature outside a school in Kelowna one afternoon. What was the temperature at 3 p.m.?
questions.explain: Find 3 p.m. on the bottom axis, go straight up to the point, then straight across to the side axis: 27 °C. A common slip is reading the point beside it (2 p.m. or 4 p.m.) instead of going straight up from the right time.

visual.caption: Temperature outside a school in Kelowna (°C)

questions.question: Ellie's line graph shows the snow that fell each day at Mount Seymour. On which day was the snowfall greatest?
questions.explain: The greatest amount is the highest point on the line, which is Thursday at 9 cm. Watch out: the flat part of the line (Tuesday to Wednesday) only means the snowfall stayed the same, and the last day is not automatically the biggest.

visual.caption: Snow that fell each day at Mount Seymour (cm)

questions.question: Maya's table of values shows that on Day 3 her bean plant was 8 cm tall. She is drawing a line graph with the day on the horizontal axis and the height in centimetres on the vertical axis. Which point should she plot?
questions.explain: A point is written (horizontal, vertical), so the day comes first and the height second: (3, 8). The most common mistake is swapping the numbers and plotting (8, 3), which puts the plant on the wrong day.

questions.question: Liam's line graph shows the money in his savings jar at the end of each month. Between which two months did the line on his graph go down?
questions.explain: The line goes down only where the next amount is smaller than the one before it: $29 in April drops to $25 in May. A line that rises less steeply (like February to March) is still going up, not down.

visual.caption: Money in Liam's savings jar at the end of each month ($)

questions.question: The line graph shows the water in a rain barrel behind a house in Surrey. How much did the water level rise from Week 1 to Week 3?
questions.explain: Read both points off the graph and subtract: 60 L − 30 L = 30 L. Two common traps are subtracting only one step of the line (45 − 30 = 15 L) or adding the two readings instead of subtracting.

visual.caption: Water in the rain barrel behind a house in Surrey (L)

questions.question: Nadia's line graph shows how many books she had finished by the end of each month. Between which two months did the number of books increase the most?
questions.explain: Compare the jumps: 8, 3, 2, then 5, so the biggest increase is September to October, where the line is steepest. The usual mistake is picking December to January just because the line is highest there — highest point is not the same as biggest change.

visual.caption: Books Nadia had finished by the end of each month

questions.question: Mr. Chen's class wants to make a line graph. Which set of data is best shown on a line graph?
options: The number of students in each of four after-school clubs
The favourite juice flavour of each student in Grade 6
The colours of the cars in the school parking lot
The height of a sunflower measured on the first day of each month
questions.explain: A line graph is for data that changes over time, so measuring one sunflower month after month fits — the line shows the growth between measurements. The other three compare separate categories, and joining category bars with a line would suggest a change that does not exist.

questions.question: The line graph shows Ravi's savings. The grid lines on the vertical axis go up by $4. How much had Ravi saved on Saturday?
questions.explain: Each space on this axis is worth $4, so halfway is $2 above $12, giving $14. The common trap is assuming every space is worth $1 and answering $12.50 or $13 — always check the labels before reading between the lines.

questions.question: Jaya rode her bike along the Galloping Goose Trail. The line graph shows her distance from home. During which 10-minute interval was she riding fastest, and how far did she ride in that interval?
questions.explain: Subtract each pair of readings to get 3 km, 2 km, 0 km and 4 km, so the steepest climb — 30 to 40 minutes — is the fastest, at 4 km. The flat part from 20 to 30 minutes means she was resting, not that she rode 5 km.

visual.caption: Jaya's distance from home on the Galloping Goose Trail (km)

questions.question: The line graph shows how much water was left in Owen's bottle during a hike near Squamish. What does the flat part of the line between 2 p.m. and 3 p.m. tell you?
options: He drank 400 mL between 2 p.m. and 3 p.m.
His bottle was empty at 3 p.m.
He drank no water between 2 p.m. and 3 p.m.
He drank all his water before 2 p.m.
questions.explain: A horizontal line means the amount stayed the same, so the bottle still held 400 mL and Owen drank nothing in that hour. The usual mistake is thinking a flat line means "nothing left" — empty would be a line sitting on 0 mL.

visual.caption: Water left in Owen's bottle during the hike (mL)

questions.question: A candle is lit, and the line graph shows its height as it burns. If the candle keeps burning at the same rate, how tall will it be at 50 minutes?
questions.explain: The line drops a steady 3 cm every 10 minutes, so from 15 cm at 30 minutes you subtract 3 cm twice: 15 − 3 − 3 = 9 cm. A common error is stopping one step early at 40 minutes (12 cm) — count the intervals carefully before extending the line.

questions.question: A Richmond class made a line graph of the total number of cans they had collected so far for the food bank, one point at the end of each week. In which week did the class collect the most cans?
questions.explain: Because the graph shows running totals, you must subtract to find each week's collection: 20, 45, 15 and 20 cans, so Week 2 was the best week. The trap is choosing Week 4 because the point is highest — with a total, the highest point only means the most cans altogether.

visual.caption: Total cans collected so far for the food bank
